# When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling

###### Abstract

Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical
reasoning tasks but remain unreliable on challenging instances. Existing
test-time scaling methods, such as repeated sampling, self-correction,
and tree search, improve performance at the cost of increased
computation, yet often exhibit diminishing returns on hard problems. We
observe that output disagreement is strongly correlated with instance
difficulty and prediction correctness, providing a useful signal for
guiding instance-level strategy selection at test time. Based on this
insight, we propose a training-free framework that formulates test-time
scaling as an instance-level routing problem, rather than allocating
more computation within a single strategy, dynamically selecting among
different scaling strategies based on output disagreement. The framework
applies lightweight resolution for consistent cases, majority voting for
moderate disagreement, and rewriting-based reformulation for highly
ambiguous instances. Experiments on seven mathematical benchmarks and
three models show that our method improves accuracy by 3%–7% while
reducing sampling cost compared to existing approaches.

## 1 Introduction

Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved high performance on
mathematical reasoning benchmarks such as Olympiad problems
\[[37](#bib.bib21), [28](#bib.bib22), [9](#bib.bib23)\], yet struggle
with challenging instances. A common direction is test-time scaling,
which allocates additional computation at inference time to improve
output quality. Representative approaches include repeated sampling
\[[33](#bib.bib1), [22](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25),
[13](#bib.bib30)\], self-correction \[[29](#bib.bib26), [7](#bib.bib27),
[23](#bib.bib28), [20](#bib.bib31), [2](#bib.bib37)\], and tree search
methods \[[38](#bib.bib32), [39](#bib.bib33), [4](#bib.bib34),
[12](#bib.bib35)\]. While effective, these approaches often suffer from
diminishing returns as computation increases \[[35](#bib.bib2)\],
suggesting that computation is not effectively allocated across
instances of varying difficulty. Most existing methods primarily focus
on adaptively allocating computation within a single strategy, with
limited attention to selecting among different strategies.

Therefore, a key challenge is not only how to allocate computation, but
also how to select appropriate inference strategies for different
instances. Among various test-time scaling strategies, rewriting has
been shown to be an effective approach for enhancing model performance
without retraining, based on the observation that model outputs are
highly sensitive to variations in problem formulation. Prior work has
explored this idea from different perspectives. [Zhou et al.
\[45\]](#bib.bib3) improves robustness via rewriting combined with a
voting mechanism. [Zhang et al. \[43\]](#bib.bib4) applies rewriting as
a preprocessing step before code generation. More recently, [Lai et al.
\[21\]](#bib.bib5) further enforces consistency across prompt
formulation, expression, and language style to stabilize model behavior.

Figure 1: The effect of rewriting and majority voting (6 samplings) for
Qwen3-8B across instances of different difficulty levels. Easy instances
are defined as those correctly answered in a single sampling, while hard
instances are those incorrectly answered in a single sampling.

However, while rewriting is effective, it is not universally beneficial.
It may alter the semantic meaning of the original instance or introduce
incorrect assumptions during reformulation. As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
rewriting degrades performance on easy instances, while it consistently
improves accuracy on hard instances. In contrast, majority voting
achieves strong performance on easy instances, but degrades on hard
instances. We further observe a strong relationship between instance
difficulty, output disagreement, and prediction correctness: hard
instances tend to exhibit higher output disagreement, whereas easy
instances usually produce more consistent results. Moreover, instances
with severe disagreement under majority voting, characterized by a flat
distribution over multiple answers, are highly correlated with incorrect
predictions. This observation indicates that output disagreement
reflects the model’s uncertainty under stochastic sampling, providing a
natural signal for guiding strategy selection. In particular, when model
outputs are highly consistent, instances are typically easier and
majority voting is sufficient; whereas under high disagreement,
instances are more likely to be challenging, making rewriting more
effective. This reveals a clear performance trade-off between majority
voting and rewriting-based strategies and motivates selecting
appropriate inference strategies based on model disagreement.

Based on this finding, we design a training-free framework without
fine-tuning or external models. Rather than introducing new reasoning
modules, our framework formulates test-time scaling as an instance-level
decision problem, determining which strategies should be applied under
different uncertainty conditions. The framework operates by routing
instances to different strategies based on the degree of model
disagreement, which we interpret as a proxy for uncertainty under
stochastic sampling. In the first stage (Disagreement Filter), we
identify no-disagreement instances via a two-sampling consistency check.
These instances are directly resolved without additional sampling or
rewriting, avoiding unnecessary computation. In the second stage (Vote
Resolve), instances with minor disagreement are further sampled and
resolved via majority voting over multiple generations, leveraging
increased sampling to improve reliability. In the final stage (Rewrite &
Rethink), instances with persistent disagreement are rewritten and
re-sampled to escape inconsistent reasoning. This framework selects
appropriate strategies for different uncertainty levels, improving
efficiency by avoiding redundant computation on easy cases while
focusing resources on ambiguous one.

We conduct experiments on seven mathematical benchmarks and three LRMs.
The results demonstrate that our method improves mathematical reasoning
accuracy by 3%–7% absolute, with particularly strong gains on
challenging benchmarks where the base models perform poorly. Moreover,
our method achieves these improvements while using fewer samplings on
the evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the generalization ability
of our method on code generation tasks. Finally, we provide an analysis
of each component, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed design
and the role of rewriting in improving robustness.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Test-Time Scaling For Math Reasoning

Test-time scaling increases inference-time computation to improve answer
quality and has been shown effective for mathematical reasoning
\[[17](#bib.bib43), [40](#bib.bib41)\]. Representative approaches
include repeated sampling \[[33](#bib.bib1), [22](#bib.bib24),
[25](#bib.bib25), [13](#bib.bib30), [41](#bib.bib36)\], self-correction
\[[11](#bib.bib29), [29](#bib.bib26), [7](#bib.bib27), [23](#bib.bib28),
[20](#bib.bib31)\], and tree search \[[38](#bib.bib32),
[39](#bib.bib33), [4](#bib.bib34), [12](#bib.bib35)\]. These methods
improve reliability via multiple outputs or iterative refinement. Recent
work \[[1](#bib.bib39), [31](#bib.bib38), [44](#bib.bib40),
[34](#bib.bib42), [18](#bib.bib44), [14](#bib.bib45)\] also studies
adaptive test-time compute allocation and compute-accuracy trade-offs,
which are complementary to our focus on routing among inference
strategies.

### 2.2 Rewriting

Rewriting has been widely studied in both information systems and
language model reasoning. In database systems, query rewriting is used
to improve retrieval efficiency \[[27](#bib.bib10)\]. Recent work
extends this idea to LLMs. RewriteLM \[[30](#bib.bib11)\] combines
instruction tuning and reinforcement learning to optimize rewrite
quality, while LLM-R2 \[[24](#bib.bib12)\] learns to distinguish
semantically equivalent but more effective rewrites via contrastive
training. Other studies explore prompt optimization and preference-based
rewriting \[[19](#bib.bib13), [5](#bib.bib14)\].

In mathematical reasoning, [Zhou et al. \[45\]](#bib.bib3) demonstrate
that surface form significantly affects model performance and propose
SCoP, which applies paraphrasing with self-consistency. [Zhang et al.
\[43\]](#bib.bib4) adopt a rewrite-then-execute strategy to improve
robustness, while [Lai et al. \[21\]](#bib.bib5) enforce
multi-dimensional consistency across prompts and expressions. These
works highlight rewriting as an effective way to improve reasoning
stability and generalization. However, these methods primarily focus on
improving single-pass generation quality, and do not explicitly address
uncertainty-aware computation allocation during inference.

## 3 Methodology

Figure 2: This figure illustrates the overall workflow of our method,
where MDD, NDS, MDS, and SDS stand for Minimal Disagreement Detector, No
Disagreement Samples, Minor Disagreement Samples, and Severe
Disagreement Samples, respectively. The four model blocks in the figure

Our method is illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
and consists of three stages: Disagreement Filter, Vote Resolve, and
Rewrite & Rethink. We employ two minimal disagreement detectors to
partition samples into three categories based on the degree of
divergence, namely No Disagreement Samples, Minor Disagreement Samples,
and Severe Disagreement Samples. Majority voting is applied to Minor
Disagreement Samples, while rewriting is used for Severe Disagreement
Samples, and the corresponding results are updated in the global answer.

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Sample Categorization via the Minimal Disagreement Detector ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
provides a step-by-step procedure of how each sample is processed in our
framework.
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Sample Categorization via the Minimal Disagreement Detector ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
defines the minimal disagreement detector and the sample categorization.
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Iterative Filtering Strategy ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
describes the first two stages, including how samples are filtered and
partitioned, as well as how iteration steps are determined.
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rewriting And Rethinking Mechanism ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
details how final answers for Severe Disagreement Samples are obtained
via rewriting.

### 3.1 Sample Categorization via the Minimal Disagreement Detector

We sample each instance $`n`$ times and obtain $`n`$ model-generated
answers, denoted as $`\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}\}`$. When the
distribution of sampled answers is highly concentrated, i.e., one answer
$`A`$ dominates, majority voting can reliably select $`A`$ as the final
prediction, indicating strong model consensus. In contrast, a flat
distribution with no dominant answer suggests significant disagreement
among model outputs, implying unreliable predictions and reduced
effectiveness of majority voting.

To exploit this observation, we propose a minimal disagreement detector
(MDD), which performs two samplings to obtain $`a_{1}`$ and $`a_{2}`$.
If $`a_{1}\neq a_{2}`$, the sample is identified as exhibiting
disagreement; otherwise, it is considered consistent. Answer equivalence
is determined using a normalized matching procedure that accounts for
numerical, structural, and symbolic equivalence (see
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Answer Equivalence Checking ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")).
As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
consistent samples are directly accepted without rewriting. This design
is motivated by the observation that rewriting is beneficial for hard
instances, while providing limited gains for easy ones
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")).
Therefore, MDD is designed to maintain high recall of correct
predictions while providing a lightweight decision rule for choosing
between majority voting and rewriting based on disagreement degree.
Table [7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
further shows that increasing the number of consistency checks reduces
recall of correct instances, motivating the use of a two-sampling design
for efficiency.

We perform multiple independent evaluations of each sample using MDD.
Let $`d_{i}`$ denote the number of detected disagreements for the i-th
sample $`S_{i}`$. Each disagreement is computed independently within one
stage from a single pairwise comparison, without comparing answers
across different stages. Based on $`d_{i}`$, samples are categorized
into three groups:

No Disagreement Samples (NDS): $`d_{i}=0`$. No disagreement is observed,
indicating stable model behavior; these samples are directly accepted
without additional computation.

Minor Disagreement Samples (MDS): $`d_{i}=1`$. A single disagreement is
observed, indicating moderate uncertainty; additional sampling is
required to improve reliability.

Severe Disagreement Samples (SDS): $`d_{i}\geq 2`$. Multiple
disagreements indicate highly unstable predictions. The answer
distribution is flat, making it difficult to obtain a reliable result by
simply increasing the number of samplings. In such cases, sampling alone
is insufficient, and rewriting is required to reformulate the input
before re-reasoning.

To better illustrate the relationship between disagreement level and
correctness, we further quantify the relationship between disagreement
level and correctness via $`P(\text{correct}\mid\text{NDS/MDS/SDS})`$ in
Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
showing a strong negative correlation between disagreement and accuracy.
This suggests that disagreement is a reliable signal for distinguishing
samples with different levels of difficulty.

### 3.2 Iterative Filtering Strategy

To efficiently allocate computational resources, we adopt an iterative
filtering strategy that categorizes samples into NDS, MDS, and SDS, and
applies rewriting only to SDS, where majority voting is insufficient. To
justify this strategy allocation, we compare baseline answering,
majority voting, and rewriting within each partition in
Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
showing that different disagreement levels favor different strategies.
We further analyze rewriting behavior in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
where rewriting is most effective on hard samples. Since rewriting is
applied to SDS, these samples should retain a high recall of incorrect
cases. As shown in
Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
increasing iterations reduces error recall while increasing cost, so we
use two iterations to balance effectiveness and efficiency.

As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
during the first iteration (Disagreement Filter), the model performs two
samplings for all samples and selects one of the sampling results to
record as a provisional answer in the global answer, which maintains the
current best answer for each sample and is updated via stage-wise
overwriting. Simultaneously, the two sampling results are checked by the
MDD. Samples with consistent answers are categorized as NDS, and their
answers in the global answer remain unchanged. The remaining samples
proceed to the second iteration.

During the second iteration (Vote Resolve), the model performs two
samplings for each remaining sample and continues to use the MDD to
check consistency. Samples showing agreement in this round are
categorized as MDS. For these MDS, majority voting is applied to all
available sampling results (i.e., the two from the first iteration plus
the two from the second, making four in total) to determine the final
answer, which is then updated in the global answer. The remaining
inconsistent samples are categorized as SDS. These samples proceed to
the next stage (Rewrite & Rethink), where the final answer is determined
via rewriting followed by re-reasoning.

### 3.3 Rewriting And Rethinking Mechanism

After the iterative filtering stage, the remaining samples are marked as
SDS, indicating that the generated answers exhibit a high degree of
uncertainty. For such samples, it is difficult to derive a reliable
answer through majority voting. We therefore employ rewriting to
determine the final answer. This method requires neither additional
training nor the introduction of external models. Instead of generating
additional reasoning paths, the model is prompted to reformulate the
problem and reattempt solving it from an alternative formulation of the
problem.

We apply the rewriting prompt template shown in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
to each SDS for a single rewrite, generating a rewritten set
$`S_{rewrite}`$. The rewriting step aims to reformulate the surface
expression of the problem while preserving its underlying semantics and
final answer. For each sample in $`S_{rewrite}`$, we perform a single
sampling to obtain an answer $`a_{rewrite}`$, which is recorded in the
global answer. By altering the surface form of the problem, this process
encourages the model to reconsider the task from a different
perspective, helping it escape previously incorrect reasoning
trajectories. With minimal additional computation, it can significantly
improve accuracy.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Settings

We evaluate our approach on seven widely used mathematical reasoning
benchmarks, including GSM8K \[[8](#bib.bib6)\], Math500
\[[16](#bib.bib15)\], Gaokao2023en \[[42](#bib.bib17)\], Olympiadbench
\[[15](#bib.bib16)\], AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25, using three base models
(Qwen3-4B \[[32](#bib.bib7)\], Qwen3-8B, and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B \[[10](#bib.bib8)\]). We use accuracy of
the final answers as the evaluation metric.

To better understand the performance of our method, we compare with four
representative methods: majority voting, dynamic voting
\[[35](#bib.bib2)\], Best-of-N with an outcome reward model, and SCoP
\[[45](#bib.bib3)\]. The first three are abbreviated as Majority, DV,
and BoN. For fair comparison, we define a sampling as any base model
generation, including both reasoning and rewriting, and constrain all
methods to six samplings per instance. Our method uses at most six
samplings per instance (2 for stage-1, 2 for stage-2, 1 for rewriting,
and 1 for re-reasoning). The Majority method samples six times per
instance and selects the final answer through simple voting; the DV
method allows up to six samplings per instance and selects the final
answer through a confidence-based voting mechanism with a threshold of
0.7, selected based on a threshold sensitivity analysis
(Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"));
BoN also samples six times per instance, then uses the
Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B-40M \[[26](#bib.bib9)\] model as an
outcome reward model to score each answer and choose the one with the
highest reward as the final answer; SCoP, on the other hand, applies one
round of problem rewriting to all instances, followed by five rounds of
sampling, and selects the final answer through simple voting. We use
temperature 0.6, top-$`p`$ 0.95, and top-$`k`$ 20, and run three seeds
(0, 42, 777). Experiments are conducted under 8K and 16K contexts
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Rewriting And Rethinking Mechanism ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
and
[5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"))
on the Qwen2.5-Math¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2.5-Math](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2.5-Math)
framework with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We further evaluate our method on a
larger-scale model (Qwen3-32B) on a subset of benchmarks to verify
scalability, with results shown in
Table [11](#A2.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").

### 4.2 Main Results

The main experimental results are shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Rewriting And Rethinking Mechanism ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").
Our method outperforms baselines on almost all benchmarks across three
models, achieving the highest average accuracy. Through experiments, we
find that significant improvements are achieved on all benchmarks except
GSM8K, while on GSM8K, the performance changes of Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B
are not as pronounced as those of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. This is
because Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B already achieve high scores on GSM8K, with
only about 5% of samples answered incorrectly, indicating that GSM8K
contains only a small fraction of samples that cause the model to
disagree. As shown in
Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Experimental Results ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on the GSM8K benchmark, the SDS after two
rounds of iterative filtering account for only 1.5% to 2% of the total
samples, making rewriting yield almost no improvement; in contrast, for
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, SDS constitute 16% of the total samples,
suggesting that the quantity of SDS influences the effectiveness of
rewriting to some extent.

In addition, we record the number of samplings used in the experiments.
We observe that, across three models, our method requires significantly
fewer samplings than other methods while achieving comparable or even
higher accuracy. We select three benchmarks (Math500, Olympiad, and
AIME24) for illustration and visualize the results in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").
On Math500 and Olympiad, our method uses approximately 40% to 60% of the
maximum sampling budget, and even on the more challenging AIME24, it
uses only about 70% of the maximum sampling budget. We also show in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
the average output tokens and wall-clock time for each sample.

### 4.3 Method Generalization Evaluation

To examine whether our method is limited to mathematical reasoning
tasks, we further evaluate it on code generation tasks using the same
hyperparameters as in the mathematical reasoning experiments.
Specifically, we keep all sampling strategies and context lengths
identical to those used in the math experiments to ensure a fair and
consistent comparison. We adopt EvalPlus²² 2
[https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus)
as the evaluation framework and assess three models (Qwen3-8B,
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct
\[[36](#bib.bib18)\]), on two code generation benchmarks (HumanEval
\[[6](#bib.bib19)\] and MBPP \[[3](#bib.bib20)\]), as well as their
enhanced variants (HumanEval+ and MBPP+).

In contrast to mathematical reasoning tasks, for code generation tasks
we do not directly use answer equality as the criterion for
disagreement; instead, we assess disagreement based on functional and
logical equivalence of the generated programs. This approach accounts
for the fact that two programs can produce the same correct results even
if their implementations differ syntactically. Specifically, we evaluate
consistency by executing both programs on the same set of test cases. If
the outputs of the two programs match exactly across all test cases, we
consider them functionally and logically equivalent. The experimental
results are presented in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").

| Method       | Math500 | Olympiad | AIME24 |
| ------------ | ------- | -------- | ------ |
| Baseline     | 84.4    | 46.4     | 36.7   |
| OnlyRewrite  | 90.4    | 59.0     | 56.7   |
| OnlyMajority | 87.6    | 48.6     | 40.0   |
| Full Method  | 92.8    | 61.9     | 66.7   |

## 5 Analysis and Discussion

### 5.1 Ablation Study

To verify the contribution of each component in our framework, we
conducted an ablation study on the Qwen3-8B. We sequentially present the
experimental results of four settings: the model without any component
(Baseline), the version with only the rewriting component (OnlyRewrite),
the version with only the majority voting component (OnlyMajority), and
the complete framework with all components integrated (Full Method).

As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Method Generalization Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling"),
when applying only the rewriting mechanism OnlyRewrite, the model shows
a significant improvement over the baseline, especially on more
challenging benchmarks such as Olympiad and AIME24. This indicates that
rewriting is more effective on difficult problems that tend to cause
disagreement. The OnlyMajority also improves over the baseline, but the
improvement is less pronounced than that of OnlyRewrite, likely because
majority voting struggles to effectively resolve highly ambiguous or
difficult samples with severe disagreement, whereas rewriting
demonstrates stronger efficacy on such samples. In contrast, for easier
problems, majority voting can often achieve high accuracy without
rewriting, highlighting the task-dependent nature of each component.
When combining both the rewriting and majority voting mechanisms, the
method achieves the best performance, highlighting the synergy between
the two components: the rewriting module improves accuracy on
challenging tasks, while the majority voting mechanism filters out noise
generated from ambiguous samples. Together, they enable the framework to
achieve comprehensive improvements in both accuracy and reasoning
stability.

To further evaluate the robustness of our method under different
sampling budgets, we conduct additional experiments on Math500 with
Qwen3-8B using 4 and 8 samplings, as shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Method Generalization Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").
To accommodate different budgets, we accordingly adjust the number of
iterations in our framework. Specifically, under the 4-sampling setting,
our method performs one iteration (two samplings) followed by a Rewrite
& Rethink step, while under the 8-sampling setting, it performs three
iterations (six samplings) followed by a Rewrite & Rethink step.

### 5.2 Analysis of Rewriting Applicability

We categorize the change in correctness before and after rewriting into
three cases: Effective Rewriting (the rewrite turns an incorrect answer
into a correct one), Ineffective Rewriting (the rewrite leaves an
incorrect answer unchanged), and Harmful Rewriting (the rewrite turns an
originally correct answer into an incorrect one). In addition, we
provide representative cases in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Case Study ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling").
We further analyze this categorization, as shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Harmful Rewriting ‣ 5.2 Analysis of Rewriting Applicability ‣ 5 Analysis and Discussion ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
(Left).

#### Effective Rewriting

We observe that most samples that can be successfully corrected through
rewriting are not originally wrong due to insufficient computational
ability, but rather because the problems contain implicit conditions or
structural information (hidden info error). These hidden elements often
cause the model to oscillate during the reasoning process: it struggles
to quickly and accurately identify the underlying mathematical
relationships and fails to stabilize on a correct solution path. In some
cases, the model even constructs an incorrect equation early in the
reasoning process due to overlooking implicit constraints.

The rewriting mechanism makes such hidden information explicit,
restructures the problem statement, or directly provides a solution
strategy. This substantially reduces the analytical burden required for
reasoning, allowing the model to enter the computation phase without
lengthy deliberation. The improvement is particularly significant on
OlympiadBench, where many problems require long token sequences for
structural parsing. Rewriting effectively compresses this reasoning
chain, leading to notable gains in accuracy.

#### Ineffective Rewriting

In another class of cases, rewriting offers no improvement. The errors
in these situations primarily stem from: answer formats that do not
conform to the required specifications (answer format error); the loss
of context or intermediate variables in long reasoning chains (context
loss error); and arithmetic errors in the calculation steps, such as
incorrect orders of magnitude in astrophysics or microscopic atomic
calculations (calculation error). These errors do not originate from
implicit information in the problem statement. Therefore, even if
rewriting provides a clearer version of the problem, the model is still
likely to repeat the same formatting or arithmetic errors during its
entire reasoning process.

#### Harmful Rewriting

In our experiments, we find that rewriting is not always effective and
can even cause originally correct answers to become incorrect. We
identify an important reason for this: the original question is already
simple, but the rewritten version compresses the text excessively,
removing or obscuring key conditions, which leads the model to reason
incorrectly (over-compression error). Therefore, avoiding rewriting
short and clear questions reduces the negative impact of rewriting.

We further compare the overall effectiveness and harmfulness of
rewriting between SCoP and our method, as shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Harmful Rewriting ‣ 5.2 Analysis of Rewriting Applicability ‣ 5 Analysis and Discussion ‣ When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling")
(Right). These results indicate that our disagreement-based routing
strategy more effectively identifies when rewriting should be applied,
increasing effective rewrites while reducing harmful ones.

Figure 5: (Left) Effective and harmful rewriting ratios across different
error types. (Right) Comparison between SCoP and our method on Qwen3-8B
across Math500, Gaokao English, and OlympiadBench. Our method achieves
higher effective and lower harmful rewriting rates.

## 6 Conclusion

This work proposes a training-free framework that formulates test-time
scaling as an instance-level strategy routing problem, using model
disagreement as a lightweight signal to guide the selection of inference
strategies. By dynamically routing instances to different strategies,
the framework applies more appropriate strategies to uncertain samples
while avoiding unnecessary or harmful processing on easier ones. We
evaluate our method on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks using
three models. The results show that it consistently improves accuracy
while requiring fewer sampling runs than existing methods. We further
examine the applicability of the framework to code generation tasks and
provide an analysis of when rewriting is beneficial or detrimental.

## Appendix A Limitations

This work leaves room for further exploration in certain aspects.

- •
  Our framework relies on output disagreement as a proxy for
  uncertainty, which may not fully capture all failure modes. In
  particular, cases with consistent but incorrect reasoning (false
  agreement) remain challenging.
- •
  The effectiveness of rewriting is instance-dependent. While our
  routing strategy reduces harmful rewriting, it cannot fully eliminate
  cases where rewriting introduces deviations from correct reasoning.
- •
  Our method currently focuses on routing among a limited set of
  test-time scaling strategies. Extending the framework to incorporate a
  broader range of strategies (e.g., search-based or verification-based
  methods) remains an open direction.

## Appendix D Answer Equivalence Checking

To determine whether two answers are equivalent, we adopt a hierarchical
matching procedure that goes beyond exact string matching.

#### Normalization.

We first normalize both prediction and reference by removing formatting
artifacts such as extra whitespace, brackets, and casing differences.
Structured outputs are converted into consistent canonical forms.

#### Numerical Equivalence.

When both answers can be parsed as numeric values, we perform
tolerance-based comparison. We additionally account for common
variations such as percentage and scale transformations (e.g., $`x`$,
$`x/100`$, and $`100x`$).

#### Structural Matching.

For structured outputs such as tuples, lists, and matrices, we perform
element-wise comparison recursively.

#### Symbolic Equivalence.

When numerical comparison is not applicable, we apply symbolic matching.
In particular, equations are first normalized into residual forms (e.g.,
$`x=y`$ to $`x-y=0`$) before symbolic equivalence checking.

This hierarchical procedure allows us to capture a broad class of
mathematically equivalent answers beyond strict string matching, while
remaining efficient in practice.
